summary: This part of the Privacy Enhanced Mail series describes three services, key certification, certificate revocation list storage, and revocation list retrieval. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This paper describes how to vouch for someone's key, and how to publish a list of keys that should no longer be trusted. It is historic.

subtitle: How Privacy-Enhanced Mail users asked a certification authority to sign their key, and to store and fetch revocation lists, all by email.

tldr.problem: Privacy-Enhanced Mail users needed a way to get their public key certified, and to store and retrieve certificate revocation lists, using only electronic mail.
tldr.mechanism: Each of three services is an email request and an email reply. Most requests and replies are ordinary RFC 1421 privacy-enhanced messages, and the CRL-retrieval request uses a new process type, CRL-RETRIEVAL-REQUEST.
tldr.outcome: The replies can be processed like any other privacy-enhanced message, so certificates and CRLs drop into the user's database. The RFC is marked Historic.

today: RFC 1424 is marked Historic and has not been obsoleted by a later RFC. It is part of the PEM series with RFC 1421, RFC 1422 and RFC 1423.

sections.title: Three Services by Email
sections.content:
RFC 1424 is Part IV of the Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM) series. It describes three services that a certification authority of the kind defined in RFC 1422 is expected to provide: key certification, certificate-revocation list (CRL) storage, and CRL retrieval.

Each service is an electronic-mail request and an electronic-mail reply. Other services, such as certificate revocation and certificate retrieval, are left to the certification authority to define. Authorities may also accept non-electronic requests, which are outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: There are three things you can ask the office to do: vouch for your name tag, keep a list of bad name tags, and hand you that list. You ask by mail and they answer by mail.

sections.title: How the Services Work
sections.content:
Requests go to an address that the certification authority advertises, for example through an "information" service. Replies go to the address in the Reply-To: field of the request, or to the From: address if there is no Reply-To:.

For key certification, the requestor sends a self-signed certificate holding its name and public key. The authority signs a certificate only if both signatures in the request are valid. The new certificate keeps the subject name and public key, and the authority picks the issuer name, serial number, validity period and signature algorithm. The reply also includes a certification path to the RFC 1422 Internet certification authority.

For CRL storage, the authority stores a CRL only if its signature and certification path are valid, then acknowledges. For CRL retrieval, the authority returns the latest CRL of each issuer named in the request. An issuer can have more than one latest CRL if it has more than one public key.
sections.eli5: The office only stamps your name tag if your paperwork checks out, and it only files a list of bad tags if the list itself is properly signed. When you ask for a list, you get the newest one.

sections.title: Request and Reply Syntax
sections.content:
A certification request is an RFC 1421 MIC-ONLY or MIC-CLEAR message with one signer and a self-signed certificate. In that certificate, version is 0, serialNumber is arbitrary (0 is suggested), and issuer and subject are both the requestor's distinguished name. The MIC encryption algorithm must be asymmetric and the MIC algorithm must be keyless, so that anyone can verify the signature.

The certification reply is also a MIC-ONLY or MIC-CLEAR message, with the same type as the request. Its MIC-Info: field and encapsulated text are taken directly from the request. A CRL-storage request and a CRL-retrieval reply are RFC 1421 CRL-type messages (Proc-Type: 4,CRL). The CRL-storage reply is an ordinary message with no particular syntax.

The CRL-retrieval request is the one new syntax. Its process type is CRL-RETRIEVAL-REQUEST, and it has a required Proc-Type: field followed by one or more Issuer: fields, in that order, with no encapsulated text.
sections.eli5: Most of the letters use the same envelope as normal private mail. Only the request for the bad-tag list has its own special form, with the names of the offices whose lists you want.

sections.title: Why the Request Is Self-Signed
sections.content:
The self-signed certificate stops a requestor from asking for a certificate that carries another party's public key. Such an attack would let the requestor pretend to be the originator of messages signed by the other party, but only in a minor way. It matters only if the requestor does not know the message being signed and the signed part does not identify the signer.

The requestor still would not be able to decrypt messages meant for the other party.
sections.eli5: You have to sign your own name tag request, so you cannot ask the office to stamp a tag that has someone else's secret code on it.

sections.title: Patent Statement
sections.content:
The RFC includes a patent statement. This version of PEM relies on patented public key technology, covering the Diffie-Hellman, Hellman-Merkle, RSA and Hellman-Pohlig methods. Public Key Partners has exclusive sub-licensing rights to those patents, and has given written assurance that parties can obtain rights on reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms.

The Internet Society, IAB, IESG and CNRI take no position on the validity or scope of the patents.
